title: • The Role of Senolytics in Anti Aging and How Functional Medicine Uses Them - Dr Stavy Nikitopoulou
abstract:
### The Science Behind Cellular Senescence  
With the advancement of research, our understanding of cellular senescence has deepened significantly over the years. Cellular senescence is a state where cells cease to divide but retain metabolic functions. While this process is crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis and preventing tumor formation, the accumulation of senescent cells contributes to aging and various degenerative diseases.  
Senescence plays a dual role in your body. It acts as a protective mechanism against cancer, preventing potential malignancies caused by damaged DNA. However, as you age, the number of these dysfunctional cells increases, leading to chronic inflammation and tissue deterioration. This accumulation can result in a variety of age-related health issues, emphasizing the need for senolytic interventions.
## Senolytics in Anti-Aging Strategies  
Many individuals are exploring innovative approaches to slow down the aging process, and senolytics have emerged as a promising option in anti-aging strategies. By targeting and eliminating senescent cells—aging cells that contribute to inflammation and tissue dysfunction—senolytics aim to rejuvenate various bodily functions and enhance your overall well-being.
#### Q: How does functional medicine incorporate senolytics in anti-aging therapies?  
A: Functional medicine takes a holistic and personalized approach to health and wellness. In the context of anti-aging, functional medicine practitioners may use senolytics as part of a broader treatment plan that includes lifestyle changes, dietary modifications, and other therapeutic interventions. By integrating senolytic treatments, practitioners aim not only to address signs of aging but also to improve overall health by focusing on the root causes of age-related conditions. This approach can result in enhanced vitality and the prevention of chronic diseases associated with aging.
